lines.text: announced to him, replied: "I realized that I had given
birth to a mortal being." And the stoic sage advises us as
follows: "What evil is there if, while kissing your little child,
you whisper: To-morrow you may be dead? Or similarly
in speaking to your friend: To-morrow either you or I will
have vanished, perhaps, and we may never see each other
again?" Certainly by this awareness we can train ourselves
to survey as from a distance whatever happens to us, to
remain in our deepest being unmoved by any human
tragedy, so that when fate strikes us we are impervious and
invulnerable to its blows. But these stoically-minded people
are not they who mourn and whom Jesus extols as blessed.
The fact is that they do not take upon themselves the burden
of pain and sorrow; rather they flee from it by making them-
selves insensible and impassive. No, those are blessed who
willingly embrace sorrow, who bear pain; who are not
affrighted as if something most strange and offensive had
befallen them, but who realize that in their pain they are
sharing in the unfathomable pain which pierces all humanity
to its depths, and who by such realization are freed to direct
their gaze to the future; who wait for God's consolation.
"God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death
shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying
nor pain any more, for the former things have passed
away" (Rev. 21: 4). How this will come to pass, we can
have no idea; but the very renunciation of understanding is
an essential part of the attitude of waiting.
There follows the beatitude: "Blessed are the meek, for
they shall inherit the earth." We pass it over; for it does not
fit into the context, since it does not speak of the frailty, the
pain and the longings of humanity; moreover textual
tradition makes it seem likely that the verse was added later.
The subsequent verse, however, does speak of the longings
of humanity: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for
righteousness, for they shall be satisfied."
These words can be easily misunderstood, since by the
word "righteousness" we normally understand a certain
virtue, that of impartiality or integrity, moral blamelessness
